property_summary: After any call to initialize(...) on a fresh C contract, the contract's baseToken equals the _baseToken argument provided to initialize; the mutant sometimes leaves baseToken unchanged when it was previously zero, causing baseToken() != _baseToken for some inputs.

For any inputs, calling initialize on a freshly-deployed C that has baseToken==address(0) must set baseToken to the _baseToken argument (i.e. after initialize, c.baseToken() == _baseToken); the mutant conditionally skips assigning baseToken when it's zero and thus can leave baseToken unchanged for some fuzzed _baseToken values causing c.baseToken()!=_baseToken.

For any callers and any initialize parameters, if initialize is called twice the second call must revert with AlreadyInitialized(); the mutant still allows a second initialize to succeed in certain state configurations by skipping assigning baseToken only when it is zero, so the mutant can make the second call succeed (changing baseToken semantics) whereas the reference always rejects any second initialize.

For any fuzzed _baseToken address and other initialize args, calling initialize on a freshly deployed C must set baseToken() equal to the provided _baseToken; the mutant that only assigns baseToken when it is already zero can leave baseToken() unchanged for some fuzzed _baseToken, violating this rule.

For any caller and any initialize parameters, initialize must always set the contract's baseToken to the provided _baseToken (observable via public getter) when called on a freshly-deployed C that currently has baseToken == address(this) (i.e. non-zero) — the mutant that only assigns baseToken when baseToken == address(0) can leave baseToken unchanged for some fuzzed _baseToken values when baseToken is nonzero, causing a mismatch; we choose to exercise the case where the pool was pre-seeded by someone sending ETH/setting baseToken via an external call by first forcibly writing a nonzero baseToken through a second contract that SELF-DELEGATES an initialize-like preassignment (simulated by calling initialize via a helper owner) so that the reference still overwrites it with the new _baseToken while the mutant may not, causing c.baseToken() != _baseToken.

For any initialize(...) call that succeeds, the reference implementation always sets baseToken exactly to the provided _baseToken (so c.baseToken() == _baseToken); the mutant that assigns nft before baseToken can be observed to transiently or permanently expose a different baseToken after initialize for some inputs (reentrancy via ERC721 safeTransferFrom to a malicious NFT that re-enters and observes/changes state), causing c.baseToken() != _baseToken.

After a successful initialize(...) call, the contract's baseToken public getter equals the _baseToken parameter passed; the mutant that assigns nft before baseToken allows a reentrant malicious NFT token receiver to observe/alter state during initialize and can make c.baseToken() differ from the supplied _baseToken for some inputs.

For any initialize(...) call that completes successfully, the contract's public baseToken getter equals the _baseToken argument passed; the mutant that assigns nft before baseToken allows a reentrant malicious ERC721 receiver to alter/observe state during initialize and can make c.baseToken() != _baseToken for some inputs.

For any call to initialize(...), the correct contract always stores baseToken == _baseToken after initialization; the mutant moves baseToken assignment later which allows a reentrant malicious ERC721 receiver (installed as nft) to observe/alter state during initialize and can cause baseToken() to differ from the supplied _baseToken for some inputs.

For any call to initialize(...), the reference contract always stores baseToken == _baseToken after the call completes; the mutant moves the baseToken assignment later which a reentrant malicious NFT receiver can exploit during initialize to make c.baseToken() differ from the supplied _baseToken for some inputs.

For any inputs, calling initialize(...) on a fresh C instance should set initialized to true and further calls to initialize(...) must revert (prevent re-initialization); the mutant removes that revert allowing a second initialize call to succeed and overwrite state, breaking the rule.
